D.2 Local Energy Vulnerabilities Europe’s dependence on developing countries for fossil fuels and China’s dominance of advanced energy technology markets are particularly impactful for U.S. Department of War (DOW) missions that depend on local power provision in the EUCOM theater. Historically dependent on Russia for natural gas and petroleum, the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers estimates that E.U. countries meet only 40% of E.U. natural gas demand through domestic production (IOGP Europe 2025), and Europe stores less than one-quarter of its annual consumption to help meet winter demand (Bousso 2025). In a contested environment in the early spring, remaining storage could be exhausted quickly. Additionally, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) reports that the European countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development held only 11.12 billion barrels in proven crude oil reserves in 2023, just 0.72% of the global total (OPEC 2025). Following the onset of the Russia- Ukraine war, Europe developed a broad strategy to reduce reliance on Russian gas, phasing out Russian petroleum by 2027. But increased liquefied natural gas imports from countries such as the United States, Qatar, and Norway have introduced challenges, including price volatility and competition from China, which prioritizes liquefied natural gas imports (Abnett 2025). In 2024, almost half of the E.U.’s net electricity generation came from advanced energy technologies (see Figure D-2), with solar surpassing coal as the fastest-growing power source (Eurostat 2025b; Rosslowe and Petrovich 2025). 68 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Source: Eurostat 2025a Europe’s accelerated adoption of advanced energy technologies is hastening the realization of the risks outlined in this analysis, including increased foreign influence on infrastructure (see Section 4.1) and vulnerability to cyber threats (see Section 2.2). European countries face similar supply chain challenges to those of the U.S. military, including a lack of supply chain visibility and concerns about the impact of contested logistics environments on supplies. China’s control over critical materials (see Section 4.1) and its vast battery manufacturing capacity could create supply chain risks for the European nations where DOW operates. The Chinese origins of many components also add uncertainty to wide-scale cyber vulnerabilities across Europe. Moreover, during conflict, gas delivery disruptions could compound with weather events to disrupt Europe’s power ecosystem, which, in turn, can affect DOW installations that rely on this power. For example, in early 2025, a four-month period of unseasonably low wind resulted in significantly reduced output from wind turbines, forcing Germany to heavily depend on its legacy power plants to meet demand (Farhat and Wertz 2025), but this low-wind period did not degrade grid reliability because gas imports increased to cover the shortfall. In 2024, wind energy accounted for 20% of European electricity consumption (WindEurope 2025a).
